title: The Paramitas in Daily Life
speaker: Seishu John Wiley
summary: Seishu John Wiley takes up the six paramitas in daily life, drawing on Norman Fischer's The World Could Be Otherwise and Dale Wright's The Six Perfections. Seishu recounts Norman's answer that his first priority as abbot was his own happiness, then describes how a long meditation practice has opened a small space before speaking, using a moment of irritation over Seishu's wife's physical therapy visit. Suzuki Roshi's phrase "shine one corner of the world" frames the rest, along with two airport scenes: a patient ticket agent during mass cancellations, and a mother calmly containing two boys beside a pacing, angry man. Seishu closes with Robin Wall Kimmerer's words on choosing joy because the earth gives it daily.

sentences.text: Oh, thank you.
I'd have forgotten that.
Good morning, everyone, and welcome.
It's nice to see you here, some familiar faces and some new faces.
And I think, do we have one person on Zoom?
Is that Ray?
Two?
Three?
Well, okay.
Welcome and thank you for joining us.
I'm going to continue our series of talks on the paramitas, or perfections, in Buddhism.
Just to name them, they are generosity, ethical conduct, patience, joyful effort, meditation, and wisdom.
I've appreciated the talks that have come before and some of the points that have been made.
I liked that Thales reminded us that generosity isn't just to be extended to other people in our relationships, but it's also for us.
For example, if you find yourself having critical, judgmental thoughts about yourself, try to be a little bit generous about that.
And I liked that Razala reminded us that maybe the paramitas just boil down to loving kindness, which is a nice way to live if you can do that.
And I liked Chris's example that practicing the paramitas is like learning a musical instrument.
Practice over time makes a difference.
Aside from listening to a couple of Dharma talks on the paramitas, I used the same books that have already been mentioned.
This one is by Norman Fischer, The World Could Be Otherwise, Imagination and the Bodhisattva Path.
For those of you who don't know, Norman Fischer was the abbot of the San Francisco Zen Center and the founding teacher of Red Cedar Zen.
The other book is by Dale Wright, who's a professor of Buddhist studies and also a practitioner, so he's not just an intellectual Buddhist.
This is The Six Perfections, Buddhism and the Cultivation of Character.

Because many of the individual paramitas have already been discussed, and Ken did a nice job of showing us how practicing one paramita often means practicing several at the same time (generosity, for example, might take patience and wisdom and ethical conduct all at the same time), I'm going to call my talk just covering some odds and ends about the paramitas.
I'm not going to focus on one in particular.
The first thing I want to emphasize is that the paramitas also apply to us as individuals.
They're not just to be used in relationships with other people.
Your well-being and mine are not less or more important than other people's.
So generosity, patience, ethical conduct, those kinds of things should be applied in our own lives as well.
Norman Fischer talks about this in his book.
When he was elected abbot of the San Francisco Zen Center, which is a difficult, complicated job, someone asked him, "What is your priority?"
And here's what he said.
This is a quote.
*My first priority is my own happiness.*
I think some people were a bit shocked by this.
It sounds a little bit self-centered.
But he pointed out that a crabby, unhappy abbot would have a big impact on the entire organization, and, on the other hand, a happy, content abbot would make a real positive difference.
The same thing is true in our own lives.
Your happiness or your unhappiness impacts every aspect of your life.
It impacts your family life.
It impacts your work life.
It even impacts your thinking.
Norman concluded on this topic by saying, and here's another quote:
*We should all cultivate our own happiness, not for ourselves.
True happiness can never be selfish in that way, but for others.*
So you can be generous with yourself and say, "Yes, I have time to establish a regular meditation practice, even when I'm busy."
And if you do that, you can be patient with yourself.

The important thing is to establish a regular practice: to sit down in a quiet place, to pay attention, to establish a stable posture, and then pay attention to your body and your breathing and notice what arises.
Notice thoughts, notice feelings, memories.
Let them come and let them go.
And when inevitably you're sidetracked, making a grocery list or thinking about something you're going to do later in the day, kindly and gently remind yourself to come back to your body and breath.
There's no need to evaluate: am I doing a good job?
How's my practice doing compared to other people?
All that's unnecessary.
So just be kind and generous with yourself when you establish a meditation practice.
One of the things I like about Dale Wright's book is the emphasis on the creation of character over a lifetime and consciously using the paramitas as guidelines for that development.
Because it seems to me that some of us do pay attention to character development and want to try to become a certain kind of person.
And other people, either some of the time or often, just say and do whatever impulses they have and don't pay much attention to the outcome.
But either way, your character will develop over your entire life.
So I guess we each get to decide whether we want to pay attention to that and try to direct it in some way or not.

I'm not sure about this for myself, but one of the things I think has happened for me with a long meditation practice is that now, when I have the impulse to say or do something, there's usually what I would call a little space where I get to think: do I want to say that?
Do I want to do that?
Is that a good idea or not?
I am really grateful for that space, because now I'm much less likely to say something I regret or do something I regret.
And when I do, because I do sometimes make mistakes, I'm more likely to see the results and realize, "Oh, that didn't turn out very well.
I better do something about that."

As an example, a couple months ago, my wife got referred to physical therapy because she's having some balance issues, and the doctor thought it would be good for her to get some exercises to strengthen her legs and work on her balance.
I was glad for that referral.
She went to her first appointment, and when she got back I asked her how it went, and she said, "Oh, great, we worked on some exercises to reduce the pain in my shoulders."
She has a lot of arthritis in different places.
So I was pissed.
I didn't say anything, but what I thought was, god damn it, you're supposed to go there to work on your balance and strengthen your legs.
But I realized I better not say anything right now.
I just thought about it, and later in the day I said, "I'm worried about your balance, I don't want you to fall.
When you go back to your physical therapist, would you ask for some exercises to address that?"
She said, "Yeah, sure," and she did that.
So I thought, that's good, I'm glad I held my tongue and gave myself some time to think about it.
Now I'm going to switch topics a little bit.

I think many of us are upset about and worried about the big problems in the world, and they seem to be getting worse: violence, war, poverty, injustice, awful political climates in various countries, global warming.
And we wonder, what can I do?
How can I live my life and make some kind of a difference?
One of the reasons I started practice in my mid-40s was that my life was going really well, but I started to worry about the three things the Buddha talked about: illness, old age, and death.
None of those things had affected me, but I knew that sooner or later I was going to have to deal with that stuff.
At the time I thought, I have no tools for that.
I'm doing well only because my life is going well, and I better do something about this.
So that's why I started practice.
But now I would add some of these other problems to that list of three.
There's lots to be worried about in the world.
How do we live our day-to-day lives and try to make some kind of a difference?
I'm going to come back to that question in a minute, but I want to tell you a little story first, which is related to the question.
When I first met my wife, she had a housemate, an 18-year-old woman who had just moved to town to go to Western.
Her name was Karen.
Karen had always wanted to be a veterinarian, even when she was, I think, eight or nine when she first got that urge.
So she went to Western, graduated, went to Washington State, got her degree in veterinary medicine, and then came back to Bellingham and started working at some veterinary clinics.
But she also did other things.
She started a spay-neuter clinic for low-income pet owners here in Whatcom County, and then she did the same thing in Mexico.
Over the years, she's established a number of animal care programs in this area, and she's made a real difference and contribution in her field.
I think her latest thing has been a website that has health concerns for different pets and what can be done about them.
I really respect and appreciate people like that, people who have a drive to do something, and they do it, and they make a difference in the world.
We all know some of the big names in that area, like Martin Luther King and Mother Teresa.
And then there are people like Karen who have a big impact in a smaller way.
But I've often felt somewhat deficient, in a way, myself, because I've never had a drive to do that.
And at this point in my life, I probably never will.
I've even talked with Norman Fischer a couple times about it: what's wrong, or what do I need to do here?
All the times I've talked to him about that, he always said, in a kind way, without any judgment, "Well, some people have that drive and some people don't."
So, to come back to the question: how do I make a difference in the world?
How do I live my life?
One of my favorite quotes from Suzuki Roshi, the short version, is "shine one corner of the world."
And the longer quote is, "We say, to shine one corner of the world.
That is enough.
Not the whole world.
Just make it clear where you are."
To me, that means our day-to-day life, each one of us.

How you interact with your family, how you interact with people at work, when you're on the freeway driving in traffic, when you encounter a homeless person, when you're in a long line at the grocery store.
All of these are opportunities to shine your corner.
And I think this is something that's possible for each one of us.
I'm not going to make a big difference in the big problems of the world, but I can work on shining my corner of the world in my day-to-day life.
The paramitas are a great set of guidelines to keep in mind.
Another Suzuki Roshi quote that fits here is, "Accept what is as it is and help it to become its best."
That can be applied to each one of us as an individual.
But also, if you're on the freeway in a traffic jam, what's the best way to go?
Do you lay on your horn and pound the steering wheel and complain to the people in the car?
Or can you just relax your body and take a few breaths and not make a difficult situation worse?
Another advocate for this approach is Jetsuna Palmo.
I don't know if any of you have heard of her.
She's an English woman who went to India in the early 1960s by herself.
She was a young woman.
She found a teacher in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition, and she's practiced intensely for over 60 years.
She said that changing the world starts with changing ourselves and bringing those changes into our day-to-day life.
So the kinds of qualities that are mentioned in the paramitas are really helpful, to develop a heart that is generous, patient, has ethical conduct, joyful effort.
The world could really use that from each one of us.
I have a lot of gratitude for the paramitas because I feel like they're giving me a guideline to follow.

I also like to look in my day-to-day life for examples, like seeing somebody handling a challenging situation really well, or even seeing someone who's not handling it well, because either one of those things inspires me to keep going.
I don't want to be a bad example.
I want to be a good example.
And it turns out that airports are really good places to watch people.
There's a lot going on there.
So I think I'll tell you a couple stories about what we've noticed in airports in the last couple years.
A few years ago we were going on a family trip to meet our daughter in Ohio.
We always fly out of Bellingham because it's so much easier than driving to SeaTac, and our little toy airport has a much better system to go through.
So we caught an early flight to Seattle.
We get off the plane, go up to our gate, and, oh, your flight's been canceled.
We had, I think, about an hour's notice.
The flight was going to leave in about an hour, canceled.
For us and a couple hundred other people, this is not good news.
Everybody's rushing to the counter to get a new flight, and we were back in line quite a ways.
I thought to myself, I hate to be one of those ticket agents behind the counter.
They've got 200 people who are not happy, and they've got to find flights for all these people.
But there was one guy behind the counter who was just amazing.
He was patient.
He maintained a sense of humor.
He never got rattled.
He had person after person coming up to him, some of them pretty stressed and pretty unhappy, and he never lost his equanimity.
It was very impressive.
I thought, wow, that guy's really earning his money today.
Then another thing happened in the airport on another trip.
Let me just get to my notes here.
We were coming back from a trip, and we landed at SeaTac in the evening and were waiting to catch a flight to Bellingham.
We get to the gate, and the flight's delayed, and then it's delayed again and delayed again.
So we have 50 or 60 people milling around the gate wondering when this thing is going to take off.
It's pretty late in the evening.
I noticed a young woman with two little kids.
They were probably six and eight, and they were very active, wrestling each other and running around.
She was doing a super job of what I would call warmly containing them.
She was letting them do stuff, but making sure they weren't going to bother or get in other people's way.
And she never lost her patience.
I thought, well, she's probably been traveling for a good chunk of the day by herself with two little kids who, the way little boys can, really rev it up and really be active.
She was just remarkable.
At the same time, there was a guy, I don't know, in his 50s or 60s, who was really pissed.
He was pacing around and muttering, "God damn it, I'm never going to fly this airline again.
When is this thing going to go off?"
In a way, he was putting into words what many people were thinking and feeling, myself included.
I was having many of the same thoughts.
But I thought to myself, wow, I am so glad that I can sit here and be aware that I'm upset.
I'm having some of this, I'm impatient.
But I can just be quiet about it.
I can let the thoughts and feelings come and go.
I actually was kind of grateful to this guy because he was showing me that I could do that too.
But I'm really glad that I'm not him.
So I think I did a lot of meditation.
I actually do a lot of meditation when I'm waiting at the airport.
But yeah, I was really glad to be able to just notice my upset and not act on it.
So I would like to encourage you to keep the paramitas in mind as you go through your day-to-day life.
They can be very helpful.

The Buddha talked about not accepting his teachings just on faith or because you give the Buddha some kind of authority, but to try his teachings in your day-to-day life and see if they reduce suffering in you and in other people.
Life will give you an endless number of opportunities to test whether the paramitas are helpful.
So the stage is set.
I'm going to finish with a little, I guess I'd call it a quote.
I'm not sure it's a poem.
But it's from Robin Wall Kimmerer, a Native American writer and activist.
One of her books is called Braiding Sweetgrass.
It's a wonderful book about ecology and Native American culture and tradition.
So here are some of her words.
I'll just say that one more time.
*Even a wounded world is feeding us.
Even a wounded world holds us, giving us moments of joy and wonder.
I choose joy over despair, not because I have my head in the sand, but because joy is what the earth gives me daily, and I must return the gift.*
Thank you very much for listening, and that's what I have to say.
